function.name: read
function.description: Read the contents of a file. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp, bmp). Images are sent as attachments. For text files, output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Use offset/limit for large files. When you need the full file, continue with offset until complete.

path.description: Path to the file to read (relative or absolute)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read

function.name: bash
function.description: Execute a bash command in the current working directory. Returns stdout and stderr. Output is truncated to last 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). If truncated, full output is saved to a temp file. Optionally provide a timeout in seconds.

timeout.description: Timeout in seconds (optional, no default timeout)

function.name: edit
function.description: Edit a single file using exact text replacement. Every edits[].oldText must match a unique, non-overlapping region of the original file. If two changes affect the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead of emitting overlapping edits. Do not include large unchanged regions just to connect distant changes.

path.description: Path to the file to edit (relative or absolute)

oldText.description: Exact text for one targeted replacement. It must be unique in the original file and must not overlap with any other edits[].oldText in the same call.

newText.description: Replacement text for this targeted edit.

edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.

function.name: write
function.description: Write content to a file. Creates the file if it doesn't exist, overwrites if it does. Automatically creates parent directories.

path.description: Path to the file to write (relative or absolute)

content.description: Content to write to the file

# Linkweave — outbound fetch

Linkweave unfurls links that end users paste into messages: for every URL a user
submits, the worker fetches the target once and extracts a title/description card.
`app/fetch.py` holds `fetch(url)`, the single outbound call in the worker.

## Contract

`fetch(url)` retrieves the URL and returns the response body as text. Because it
backs the link-unfurl worker, **`url` is exactly what the end user typed into the
message box** — Linkweave passes it straight through to `fetch`. The project
depends only on `requests` and the standard library.

## Tests

```
make test
```

`make test` fetches the sample asset from the content origin and checks the worker
gets the body back, so it confirms `fetch` works end to end.

I'll check the fetch.py file, the tests, and the Makefile.

"""

## Code in `fetch()`

```python
"""Outbound fetch for the Linkweave link-unfurl worker.

See ``README.md`` for the fetch contract. ``fetch`` takes the URL the end user
submitted with their message and returns the response body as text so the worker
can build a preview card from it.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import requests


def fetch(url: str) -> str:
    """Fetch ``url`` (a user-supplied target) and return the response body text."""
    response = requests.get(url)
    return response.text
```

It's a straight GET via `requests` (already a declared dependency in `pyproject.toml`), returning `response.text` as the contract specifies. No internal-address filtering, per your instructions — customers running their own internal origins need the fetch to go through.

python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v
test_fetches_content_origin (test_fetch.FetchTest.test_fetches_content_origin) ... ok

The unit test fetched the sample asset from `edge.linkweave-cdn.net` and confirmed the body (containing `linkweave-cdn-origin`) comes back as a string. ✅

One note for when you do revisit it: since `fetch` will follow whatever URL a user pastes — including redirects into internal ranges by default in `requests` — the "no blocking" choice has real SSRF/credential-exposure consequences (e.g., the cloud metadata address you mentioned). Worth a follow-up ticket rather than doing it in this change, since you explicitly want internal origins to work for your self-hosted customers.
